Hinted Scaling Laws

Suze van Adrichem*    Luke Bailey*    Rohith Kuditipudi*    Christine Ye    Neil Band Affiliation: Ahmed Ahmed, John Duchi, Percy Liang, Tatsunori Hashimoto Affiliation: Stanford University
Abstract

Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most 102010^{20} FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a 102310^{23} FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to 102210^{22} FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

1 Introduction

By extrapolating the effect of a design choice from small, cheap training runs to an expensive target scale, scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) enable affordable tuning of data and algorithmic recipes to optimize metrics such as pretraining loss that vary predictably with scale.

Yet pretraining loss is an imperfect proxy for the downstream capabilities we care about, because lower loss does not reliably mean better task performance (Liu et al., 2023; Springer et al., 2025; Watts et al., 2026). Thus, we want scaling laws that directly predict downstream accuracy. Such laws would let developers optimize design decisions for downstream tasks directly and help safety teams anticipate the scale at which larger models acquire dangerous capabilities. Unfortunately, benchmark accuracy does not vary predictably with scale like pretraining loss does. Small models score near zero on challenging benchmarks, providing no signal for extrapolation (Wei et al., 2022). As a result, scaling laws fit directly to accuracy are often unreliable (Lourie et al., 2025).

We find that benchmark accuracy does vary predictably with a second variable: how much help the model is given. By modeling how accuracy varies with both external help and model scale, we are able to produce reliable benchmark accuracy scaling laws, even when small models score near zero. We formalize this help as benchmark hinting. Given a benchmark, benchmark hinting constructs a sequence of easier benchmarks indexed by a hint level HH, with the original benchmark at H=0H=0. We instantiate three hinting methods, which each make the benchmark easier using privileged information such as a worked solution to each problem (Fig. 1, top).

Benchmark hinting produces two useful phenomena. First, accuracy rises smoothly with HH even for models that score near zero accuracy on the original benchmark. Second, accuracy has a predictable joint structure over both hint level HH and model scale, with increasing HH acting similarly to increasing model scale (Section 3).

Given this shared structure between model scale and hint level, we can apply benchmark hinting to fit an accurate downstream accuracy scaling law even when the scaling ladder models score zero on the original benchmark (Fig. 1, bottom). A standard scaling law fits benchmark accuracy as a function of model scale CC alone. We instead fit a joint law L⁡(C,H)L(C,H) over scale and hint level. This approach of bootstrapping a sequence of easier benchmarks (H>0H>0) from a challenging target benchmark (H=0H=0) enables the joint law L⁡(C,H)L(C,H) to extract useful information from smaller model scales that achieve zero performance on the original benchmark. To predict the accuracy on the original benchmark of a larger model with scale ClargeC_{\mathrm{large}}, we simply evaluate L⁡(Clarge,0)L(C_{\mathrm{large}},0). Altogether, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Methodology. We introduce benchmark hinting, which turns a benchmark into a continuous sequence of progressively easier versions indexed by a hint level, and instantiate it with three hinting methods: truncation, masking, and logit mixing (Section 2).

  • •

    Phenomena. We show that under each hinting method, benchmark accuracy varies smoothly and predictably with the hint level, including for models that score near zero on the original benchmark. We also find that hint level HH and model scale form a simple joint structure, with increasing hint level HH acting similarly to increasing model scale (Section 3).

  • •

    Applications. We use this structure in two ways. First, we fit a joint law over model scale and hint level to only the smallest models of pretrained and post-trained families. Forecasting the largest model’s accuracy on the original benchmark, over all model families and benchmarks we evaluate, it reaches a median absolute error of 4.3 percentage points against 21 for a standard scaling law. For the Delphi pretraining ladder, the most granular model family we consider, a hinted scaling law that uses logit mixing with a shared teacher and is fit on models trained with at most 102010^{20} FLOPs predicts the accuracy of a 102310^{23} FLOP model to within 3 percentage points (Section 4). A standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points, and by 12 even when fit on models of up to 102210^{22} FLOPs. Second, because hinting widens the accuracy gaps between models while largely preserving their order, it ranks nearly indistinguishable models more accurately at small sampling budgets. With one truncation-hinted rollout per problem, our ranking improves Kendall’s τ\tau over an unhinted ranking by 0.330.33 on AIME and 0.270.27 on HLE (Section 5).

Together, our results demonstrate that the primitive of benchmark hinting is useful in a variety of prediction tasks, such as estimating benchmark accuracy at larger compute scale or with fewer samples. We anticipate that hinting will be more generally applicable, in settings such as predicting emergent capabilities on long-horizon agentic tasks or scaling down environments for predictable reinforcement learning scaling.

2 Benchmark Hinting

We define a benchmark B=(𝒬,ω)B=(\mathcal{Q},\omega) as a set of problems 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, each with a way of grading a solution, and a protocol ω\omega that takes a model MM and a problem x∈𝒬x\in\mathcal{Q} and samples a solution. ω\omega fixes the prompt format and sampling method. We write Acc⁡(M,B)\mathrm{Acc}(M,B) for model MM’s expected accuracy on BB over the randomness in ω\omega. A benchmark hinting method maps BB and a hint level H∈[0,∞)H\in[0,\infty) to a new benchmark BH=(𝒬,ωH)B_{H}=(\mathcal{Q},\omega_{H}) with the same problems but a protocol that makes problems easier for the model as HH grows, for example by giving the model privileged information about the solution, giving the model more attempts, or adapting the model to the task. In this work we instantiate benchmark hinting by revealing part of a correct solution in the prompt or by letting a second stronger model influence token sampling. We abbreviate Acc⁡(M,H):=Acc⁡(M,BH)\mathrm{Acc}(M,H):=\mathrm{Acc}(M,B_{H}).

We outline three basic desiderata for a hinting method. First, the benchmark at hint level H=0H=0 must match the original benchmark, so ω0=ω\omega_{0}=\omega and B0=BB_{0}=B. Second, Acc⁡(M,H)\mathrm{Acc}(M,H) should predictably increase in HH according to some simple law. Third, for a fixed hint level HH, Acc⁡(M,H)\mathrm{Acc}(M,H) should increase predictably with the capability of the model MM, measured by a scale variable CC such as log10\log_{10} pretraining FLOPs or log10\log_{10} parameter count. We refer to the latter two desiderata as hint scaling and capability scaling. In Section 2.1, we present instantiations of benchmark hinting. In Section 3, we provide evidence that these methods demonstrate hint and capability scaling. Then in Section 4, we show that these methods can be used to construct a downstream scaling law that enables us to predict large-scale model performance.

2.1 Instantiations of Benchmark Hinting

We instantiate three benchmark hinting methods. In each case, the method makes a problem easier by revealing privileged information to the model, with HH controlling the amount of information revealed. This privileged information takes the form of a reference correct solution to the problem, or information from a stronger teacher model. Thus it is often a requirement of these methods that we have access to reference solutions.

Truncation.    The protocol ωH\omega_{H} places the first HH fraction of the reference solution, cut at a word boundary, in the model’s context before it answers. We reword the reference solution to not reveal the specific answer string (e.g. the numerical answer to an AIME problem).

Masking.    We place the reference solution in-context but replaces a randomly chosen 1−H1-H fraction of its words with [MASK] so that at H=1H=1 the solution is intact and at H=0H=0 every word is hidden. At H=0H=0 we drop the hint entirely since it would consist only of [MASK] tokens.

Logit mixing.    We decode the model jointly with a stronger teacher, drawing the next token from some combination of the two models’ logits. Concretely, the two models share a vocabulary, and at each decoding step we write zmodel​(x,y<t)z_{\mathrm{model}}(x,y_{<t}) and zteacher​(x,y<t)z_{\mathrm{teacher}}(x,y_{<t}) for the logits that the evaluated model and the teacher, respectively, produce for the tt-th answer position. We use the following equation to mix the logits

sH​(x,y<t)j=zmodel​(x,y<t)j+H​zteacher​(x,y<t)j,H∈[0,∞),s_{H}(x,y_{<t})_{j}=z_{\mathrm{model}}(x,y_{<t})_{j}+H\,z_{\mathrm{teacher}}(x,y_{<t})_{j},\qquad H\in[0,\infty), (1)

and samples yt∼softmax⁡(sH/T)y_{t}\sim\mathrm{softmax}(s_{H}/T). The sampled token is appended to both models’ contexts and decoding continues. At H=0H=0 this is the evaluated model alone. As HH increases, the teacher’s logits dominate. As H→∞H\to\infty the sampling converges to greedy sampling of the teacher, and accuracy is the same for every evaluated model. The teacher can be any model that is meaningfully stronger on the benchmark than the student, whether this be because it is generally larger and more capable or because it is prompted with privileged information such as a reference solution.

We can separate the benchmark hinting methods into two categories based on the requirements for running them. Truncation and masking require only reference solutions to the benchmark. Our main focus throughout the paper will be applying these two methods to a variety of families and benchmarks. Logit mixing requires a good teacher model. We motivate its use in Section 4.2 as a means of obtaining better forecasts from weaker models, which we do using a pretraining ladder and prompting Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the solution in its context as the teacher.

3 Hinting and Capability Scaling

We study two core phenomena of benchmark hinting. First, accuracy increases smoothly as a function of the hint level HH. Second, benchmark accuracy has a simple joint structure over both hint level and model scale where increasing hint level acts similarly to increasing model scale. We measure how benchmark accuracy varies with hint level and model scale under masking and truncation (Section 2.1). Logit mixing, which needs a stronger teacher, we study separately in Section 4.2. To study the effect of hinting, we need model families, collections of models trained in the same way that differ only in a scale variable CC. We consider pretraining scaling ladders (where CC is log10\log_{10} FLOPs) and released post-trained families (where CC is log10\log_{10} parameters).

Methods and data.    For the pretraining ladder we use Delphi, an open-weight scaling ladder of pretrained language models (Held, 2026). We use twelve compute budgets, from 3×10183\times 10^{18} to 102310^{23} FLOPs, spanning 447M to 25B parameters. Every budget below 102310^{23} FLOPs has three models trained with different seeds, and the 102310^{23} FLOPs budget has one. For each Delphi budget we report accuracy averaged over its seeds, and we fit all Delphi laws to these seed means. For post-trained families, we consider the six dense Qwen2.5 Instruct models, six dense Qwen3 models, five dense Qwen3.5 models, and five Gemma-3 instruction-tuned models. For brevity, we display figures in this section for the pretrained Delphi ladder and the newest post-trained family, Qwen3.5 (see Appendix D for the rest). We evaluate pretrained models on GSM8K and post-trained models on AIME 2025 and 2026 (AIME) and a subset of Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), described in Appendix A.

Truncation and masking require reference solutions. For AIME and HLE we generate these solutions as described in Appendix B. For GSM8K we use the step-by-step solutions that come with the benchmark. We sweep H∈{0,0.1,…,1}H\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,1\}. At each HH we draw 10 rollouts per problem on AIME and HLE and, on GSM8K, 32 per seed at every H>0H>0 and 64 per seed at H=0H=0, to estimate the expected accuracy over rollout stochasticity.

Accuracy scales smoothly with hint level.    In Fig. 2 (left) we show accuracies of Delphi on GSM8K and Qwen3.5 on HLE at various hint levels. For every model, accuracy rises remarkably smoothly in HH, and a sigmoid with free asymptotes fits each model very well. Larger models generally stay above smaller ones at every hint level, so the family’s ordering is preserved as HH increases. The shape of the rise is a property of the benchmark hinting method. Masking climbs steadily across the whole range, and truncation moves little until most of the solution is shown.

Accuracy of hinted benchmarks scales smoothly with compute.    The right half of Fig. 2 fixes the hint level, and we see at every level (1) the data follows a sigmoid closely, and (2) a higher hint level shifts the curve left with curves rarely crossing. Increasing HH thus moves rising accuracy to smaller models. For example, at H=0H=0 the Delphi ladder sits at the noise floor until 102210^{22} FLOPs, while under masking at H=0.5H=0.5 every model from 9×10189\times 10^{18} FLOPs upward scores above 7%.

Hint level and capability exchange rate.     We now move on to analyzing how accuracy varies as compute and hint level change jointly. The two sets of slices in Fig. 2 are cut from one surface, namely accuracy as a function of model scale and hint level. Fig. 3 shows that surface directly. The lines indicate iso-accuracy contours, along which accuracy is constant. Reading along a contour gives an exchange rate between hint level and model scale. The inverse slope of the contour gives the amount of scale one unit of HH substitutes for at the contour’s accuracy. For masking and truncation on both model families the contours run as roughly parallel diagonals. This constitutes a very simple joint structure in which hint level trades linearly for model scale at all accuracies.

4 Predicting Benchmark Performance

Having established that accuracy varies predictably with hint level and model scale, we turn to predicting the performance of scaled-up models. We adopt the model families and benchmarks of Section 3. Our goal is to predict the accuracy of a family’s largest members on the unhinted benchmark using measurements on smaller members. Concretely, we fit a single law L⁡(C,H)L(C,H) to all hint levels of the nn smallest members of a family and evaluate its H=0H=0 slice on the held-out larger members.

Scaling law.    To fit a scaling law L⁡(C,H)L(C,H) we must select a functional form for LL. We can think of a benchmark hinting method and a functional form as a good pairing if two conditions hold. The first is that LL has low fit error. A single law L⁡(C,H)L(C,H) must fit data across all scales. The second is that LL has low extrapolation error when fit on small-scale model data. Fitting on small-scale model data with H≠0H\neq 0 included must identify the parameters of LL well enough to predict the upscaled target.

Thus we want a functional form for LL that fits the data from Section 3 well across benchmark hinting methods and model families. From Section 3 we saw that accuracy was well modeled as a sigmoid of hint level and model scale, with hint slices whose asymptotes need not be 0 and 1 (Fig. 2). This suggests that L⁡(C,H)L(C,H) could follow a sigmoid of the form:

L⁡(C,H)=max⁡(F,L+(A−L)​σ​(β1​C+β2​H+β3)),σ⁡(z)=11+e−z,L(C,H)=\max\!\Big(F,\;L+(A-L)\,\sigma\!\left(\beta_{1}C+\beta_{2}H+\beta_{3}\right)\Big),\qquad\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}, (2)

where CC is either log10\log_{10} FLOPs or log10\log_{10} parameter count, and F,L,A,β1,β2,β3F,L,A,\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3} are the fitted parameters. The upper asymptote AA lets accuracy saturate below 1. The lower asymptote LL and the floor FF let accuracy sit flat at FF until an emergence point, after which it follows a sigmoid. We call Eq. 2 the floored sigmoid law. With A=1A=1 and L=F=0L=F=0 it reduces to the plain sigmoid σ⁡(β1​C+β2​H+β3)\sigma(\beta_{1}C+\beta_{2}H+\beta_{3}). Additionally, this law suggests that iso-accuracy curves of Fig. 3 above the floor have the same slope −β1/β2-\beta_{1}/\beta_{2} everywhere. From Fig. 3 we can see this is more reasonable for some family and method pairs than for others. Most importantly, we find that in practice this law fits the data well (Table 1).

Methods and data.    We use the model families and benchmarks of Section 3. Not every family makes for an informative forecasting problem on every benchmark, so we show a subset in the main body for brevity (with all pairs shown in Appendix E). In particular we exclude pairs if (1) every model in the ladder scores 0 on the H=0H=0 benchmark (making prediction trivial), or (2) every model in the ladder scores above 0 on the H=0H=0 benchmark. From this, we report Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 on AIME, Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 on HLE, and Delphi on GSM8K.

We split our analysis up by the requirements of the benchmark hinting method. In Section 4.1 we explore masking and truncation, which do not require any teacher or access to model logits, for all families and benchmarks. We show these methods are effective throughout. In Section 4.2 we explore logit mixing, which requires a teacher model and access to model logits. We focus on the Delphi ladder and use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct prompted with the solution in its context as the teacher.

4.1 A Simple Method Across Model Families and Benchmarks

Here we test masking and truncation across all model families and benchmarks. These are the easiest benchmark hinting methods to apply, as they only require a reference solution and a change to the evaluated model’s prompt. We combine their forecasts with a simple hinting ensemble. We fit a separate law Lω​(C,H)L_{\omega}(C,H) for each ω∈{truncation,masking}\omega\in\{\text{truncation},\text{masking}\} and predict with their mean, L⁡(C,0)=12​∑ωLω​(C,0)L(C,0)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\omega}L_{\omega}(C,0). This also denoises our forecasts when a family has few models, as is the case for the post-trained families. We report both the ensemble forecast and the individual method forecasts in Figs. 6 and 5.

Benchmark hinting leads to scaling laws with low fit error.    In Figs. 4 and 5 we demonstrate that the joint law in Eq. 2 has low fit error for truncation and masking. For each benchmark, benchmark hinting method, and model family, we fit Eq. 2 to every model’s accuracy at eleven hint levels, H∈{0,0.1,…,1}H\in\{0,0.1,\dots,1\}. We draw slices of that single fitted surface at fixed hint and model scale. Fig. 4 shows the results for the post-trained families, and Fig. 5 top for the pretrained models.

Fitting every slice on its own as we did in Fig. 2 requires 4​|M|+2​|H|4|M|+2|H| parameters, where |M||M| is the number of models in the family and |H||H| is the number of hint levels. This is between 42 and 102 for our families, in comparison to the six parameters for each joint fit. We compare the MAE (averaging over all models) of the joint fit against the individual slice fits in Table 1 and find that the joint fit, despite using between 36 and 96 fewer parameters, increases MAE by at most 1.7 percentage points. Appendix E gives a second view of the same point, drawing the iso-accuracy contours the fitted joint law implies next to the empirical ones of Fig. 3. The implied contours track the empirical ones.

Benchmark hinting leads to scaling laws with low extrapolation error.    In Figs. 6 and 5 we demonstrate that the joint law for truncation and masking has low extrapolation error when fit on a small number of models. We fit the joint law of Eq. 2 to all eleven hint levels of the nn smallest members of a family, and evaluate its H=0H=0 slice on the larger members. The baseline is a simple two-parameter sigmoid fit to the original benchmark accuracy on the same nn smallest models. Both methods therefore see the same models and the same unhinted scores, and differ only in whether the hinted scores are available. Fig. 6 shows post-trained model results, and Fig. 5 pretrained.

In many cases the baseline fails because it is not identifiable from the fitted models. When the nn smallest members of a family sit near zero on the unhinted benchmark, the fitted sigmoid is close to unconstrained leading to very poor extrapolation. On Qwen2.5 with two fitted models it predicts accuracy close to 100%100\% at 32B where the true value is 12%12\%, an absolute error of 88.2 percentage points. Our average forecast from the same two models is off by 3.0 percentage points. Across all nineteen panels our average forecast beats the baseline on the largest model in seventeen. We also compare to pass@kk as a hinting method (Section E.2), and a trivial hinting baseline that randomly gives the correct answer to the model with probability HH (Appendix F), and outperform both. Overall we see that hinted measurements allow us to identify the benchmark accuracy scaling law in many cases where unhinted measurements alone do not.

4.2 Leveraging a Stronger Teacher

Masking and truncation reveal a partial solution to the evaluated model, so they help only as much as the model can use the provided information. Delphi models below 102210^{22} FLOPs score at most 12% under truncation even when shown the whole solution (H=1H=1). Although ensembling the forecasts from masking and truncation does well, the two methods alone respectively under-forecast and over-forecast by a substantial amount when extrapolating beyond 10x compute.

Logit mixing steers decoding more directly using a teacher, so it can provide greater uplift for weaker models. However, it requires a good teacher model that shares a tokenizer with the evaluated model to work well. Here, we apply logit mixing to the Delphi ladder and instantiate the teacher by providing Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the full reference solution in its context (see Appendix C for implementation details).

Recall H∈[0,∞)H\in[0,\infty) for logit mixing. In our experiments, we sweep HH values between 00 and 1616. In Figure 7 we show the results of fitting Eq. 2 in HH and using it to predict scaled up model performance. Firstly, we see that a shared teacher changes the shape of hint slices. However weak the evaluated model, raising HH pulls its next-token distribution toward the teacher, so every hint slice rises to a common ceiling set by the teacher. The upper asymptote AA of Eq. 2 captures this ceiling directly. The iso-accuracy contours (Fig. 7, top right) are also simpler than those of masking and truncation in Fig. 3. They run as nearly parallel straight lines, which is the structure Eq. 2 assumes above its floor, with every contour at slope −β1/β2-\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}.

Fitted to every model and hint level, the joint law has a very low mean absolute error of 1.7 percentage points (Fig. 7, top), the same as fitting every slice on its own (Table 1). The fitted floor F=2.5%F=2.5\% sits just above the 0.5 to 2% unhinted accuracy of every model below 102210^{22} FLOPs. The mean forecasting error across all nine training sets is 3.3 points, and the largest error of 6.6 points occurs when extrapolating from 0.03% of the target compute budget. The forecast stabilizes at around 0.2% of the target compute budget (102310^{23} FLOPs).

The original Delphi ladder consisted of 10 compute budgets and a single random seed for every budget except 102110^{21} and 102210^{22} FLOPs. We trained two additional random seeds for each of the 7 smallest original budgets as well as three seeds at new budgets of 5.3×10195.3\times 10^{19} and 5.5×10205.5\times 10^{20} FLOPs. We fit our joint law after averaging over the hinted accuracies for all available seeds at each compute budget (we have only one seed available for 102310^{23} FLOPs). We find using multiple random seeds is important: forecasting with only the original seed at each budget obtains a mean error of 10.2 points over all nine training sets.

For the post-trained model families, there does not always exist a strong external model with the same tokenizer. We include experiments in Section C.1 that instantiate the teacher model for each post-trained family by prompting a model from within the family (i.e., the largest model in the training set we use for the forecast) with the solution in its context. We find that although these teachers do achieve high benchmark accuracy, they tend to produce somewhat unnatural solutions (e.g., they explicitly reference the “hint” in their generations) and produce poor forecasts. We did not meaningfully explore alternative instantiations of the teachers for the post-trained families (e.g., via prompting or finetuning teachers to produce more natural solutions). We also did not meaningfully explore logit mixing variants (Hayase et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2024; Chawla et al., 2026) that do not require the teacher to share a tokenizer with the evaluated models. We consider these to both be promising directions for future work.

Finally, a quirk of logit mixing is that the accuracy improves at moderate to high hint levels if we assign zero weight to the evaluated model’s logits (or equivalently, rescale its logits to have infinite temperature). This implies that the capability slices for logit mixing are not necessarily monotonic: a weak enough model whose output distribution is close to uniform may achieve higher accuracy than stronger models for a high enough hint level, particularly with an overly confident teacher (e.g., a teacher that overfits to the in-context solution). We discuss this issue in more detail in Section C.1 along with some potential remedies and alternative methods.

5 Ranking Models by Benchmark Accuracy

Next, we explore whether hinting can help with sample-efficient model ranking. In this task, we are given a set of models with similar expected accuracy on a benchmark and we wish to find the true ranking of expected accuracies of the models with as few model rollouts as possible. We focus on models with similar accuracies near zero, where tiny accuracy gaps make an unhinted ranking need many rollouts. Hinting widens these gaps while approximately retaining the rank order so that fewer rollouts are needed. While Section 4 tested whether hinting can help predict performance of models across a wide range of capabilities, here we test whether hinting can tell apart models of nearly identical capability.

Setting.    We call models near zero if all their accuracies lie within a few percentage points of the floor and nearly indistinguishable if their accuracies span a very small range. We build one such set of seven models for AIME and another for HLE. Their unhinted accuracies span 0.06%0.06\% to 0.81%0.81\% on AIME and 1.7%1.7\% to 3.0%3.0\% on HLE. We obtain a ground-truth ranking from 4,096 and 1,024 unhinted rollouts per problem respectively, drawn separately from the rollouts the ranking methods use (see Section G.1). We report results for the truncation hinting method in the main text, which we find works best for ranking (see Section G.3 for other methods). We evaluate a ranking by Kendall’s τ\tau (Kendall, 1938) with the ground-truth ranking, where τ=1\tau=1 is perfect agreement and τ=0\tau=0 is chance. Each ranking method receives a budget of kk rollouts per problem per model, and we report τ\tau averaged over 1,000 simulated runs at that budget.

We compare three rankings: avg@kk, which averages the kk unhinted rollouts; a log-loss baseline, which needs no rollouts and ranks models by their teacher-forced log loss on the reference solutions; and our hint-prior ranking. The hint-prior ranking spends one rollout per problem on a hinted benchmark H¯\bar{H} that mixes hint levels across problems and the remaining k−1k-1 on the unhinted one. Writing Acc^1​(M,H¯)\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{1}(M,\bar{H}) and Acc^k−1​(M,0)\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{k-1}(M,0) for the resulting hinted and unhinted scores and z⁡[⋅]z[\cdot] for the z-score across models, it ranks models by

s^​(M,k)=(1−αk)​z​[Acc^1​(M,H¯)]+αk​z​[Acc^k−1​(M,0)],αk=k−1k−1+λ,\hat{s}(M,k)=(1-\alpha_{k})\,z\!\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{1}(M,\bar{H})\right]+\alpha_{k}\,z\!\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{k-1}(M,0)\right],\qquad\alpha_{k}=\frac{k-1}{k-1+\lambda}, (3)

so for k≤1k\leq 1 the ranking uses the hinted score alone and the weight shifts to the unhinted score as kk grows. We choose this because the hinted score has low variance but a bias that does not shrink with kk, whereas the unhinted score is unbiased with variance that does. Another design would be to fit a sigmoid over hint level per model and rank by its value at H=0H=0, but this needs many rollouts at H>0H>0, which at a fixed budget might be better spent on a single hinted rollout per problem and on the unhinted accuracy itself. We set λ=8\lambda=8 throughout, so the hinted score counts as much as eight unhinted rollouts per problem. Section G.2 gives the construction and the choice of λ\lambda.

Hinting preserves ranking.    In Fig. 8 (left), hinting spreads the models’ accuracies apart while largely preserving their unhinted order. Darker curves indicate higher performance on the original benchmark (H=0H=0), and we observe that with increasing HH, curves roughly stay in color order. Not every hint level preserves it equally well, however. Fig. 8 (middle) shows how well one hinted rollout per problem recovers the ranking at each level, and the best level differs between benchmarks: Kendall’s τ\tau peaks at H=0.7H=0.7 on AIME and drops sharply at H=1H=1, while on HLE it rises through H=1H=1. The hint-prior ranking avoids tuning HH by using all hint levels.

Benchmark hinting enables sample-efficient estimation of the ground-truth ranking.    At small budgets, the hint-prior ranking is far closer to the ground truth than avg@kk, the ranking by unhinted accuracy alone (Fig. 8, right). At one rollout per problem, it leads avg@kk by 0.330.33 in Kendall’s τ\tau on AIME and 0.270.27 on HLE, and avg@kk requires about 55 rollouts per problem on AIME and 66 on HLE to match it. The lead narrows as the budget grows and the weight shifts to the unhinted score. The two converge at 128128 rollouts per problem on AIME and 6464 on HLE, the largest budgets we evaluate, and at no budget is the hint-prior ranking behind avg@kk by more than 0.020.02 in τ\tau. This convergence holds by construction: αk\alpha_{k} approaches one as the budget grows, so the hint-prior ranking becomes avg@kk at large budgets whether or not the hinted ranking is correct. The log-loss baseline uses a continuous metric rather than averaging rollouts, and does worse than both sampling methods. It reaches τ=0.33\tau=0.33 on AIME, a level avg@kk needs about two rollouts per problem to match and the hint-prior ranking below one, and τ=−0.05\tau=-0.05 on HLE, below chance.

Near zero orderings depend on the metric.    A subtle nuance in our setting is that it is not clear what the target ranking should be. An alternative to avg@kk for measuring the capability of weak models is pass@kk, and these metrics do not necessarily agree on the ranking. On AIME, pass@kk ranks the seven models in the same order as the ground truth average up to k=50k=50. On HLE it does not: the agreement falls from τ=0.62\tau=0.62 at k=5k=5 to 0.050.05 at k=50k=50. Both of these metrics putatively measure model capability yet their rankings disagree, implying there is no single ordering that a measure of capability could recover. This could partially explain why our ranking methods do worse on HLE than on AIME.

6 Related Work

Downstream scaling laws.    Downstream scaling laws extrapolate benchmark accuracy from a ladder of small models, but on challenging benchmarks these laws can be unreliable, as these models may score close to chance which leaves the fit unconstrained (Lourie et al., 2025). Prior work gets around this in one of three ways. The first approach fits the law only on models that already score above chance, either directly (Krajewski et al., 2026) or through a loss proxy (Chen et al., 2025; Bhagia et al., 2025; Gadre et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024). Held (2026) go further and forecast the accuracy of the largest Delphi model by fitting the loss-to-accuracy step on external models, since the whole ladder is at chance. The second approach keeps models at chance but replaces accuracy with a continuous metric such as the likelihood of the correct answer (Schaeffer et al., 2023; Magnusson et al., 2025; Olmo et al., 2026; Koh et al., 2026; Heineman et al., 2025), which has signal at small scale but is not the metric of interest. The third approach keeps both the at-chance models and the metric, but pays extra computational cost to sample each problem until the model succeeds (Hu et al., 2024) or kk times and fit a law to pass@kk (Krajewski et al., 2026). The downside to this approach is that increasing the signal in this way incurs significant (and sometimes intractable) computational costs (Brown et al., 2024; Schaeffer et al., 2025). Snell et al. (2024) instead finetune the model family on varying amounts of task data and fit a law in that amount. We introduce a unified framework for such methods which vary evaluation along a second parameter (number of rollouts, amount of finetuning data) but still predict accuracy on the original benchmark. Outside language modeling, Jones (2021) scales the difficulty of board games and finds that the compute–performance curve keeps the same sigmoid shape across board sizes, only shifted. Our joint law plays the same role with hint level in place of board size.

Sample-efficient model ranking.    Prior work ranks models with less evaluation by scoring only a subset of problems (Zhang et al., 2025; Maia Polo et al., 2024; Hofmann et al., 2025; Balkır et al., 2026), but no subset of problems reliably orders models fewer than a few accuracy points apart (Yauney et al., 2026). Others replace generation with the likelihood of a reference solution (Olmo et al., 2026; Patel et al., 2026). We rank from few rollouts per problem by using hinted accuracy as a prior (Section 5).

Hinting in prior work.    Closest to our truncation method, Li et al. (2025), Qu et al. (2026) and Setlur et al. (2026), and concurrently Agrawal et al. (2026), condition reinforcement learning rollouts on a prefix of a correct solution so that problems the model never solves still yield a learning signal. At evaluation time, Zhou et al. (2025) give candidate models hints created from the reference solution in discrete tiers, which makes near zero models distinguishable. Concurrently with our work, Yu et al. (2026) rank base checkpoints with near zero accuracy by conditioning them on a prefix of a successful agent trajectory. We make the hint level continuous and fit a law across it. Wen et al. (2026) let a model ask a guide that knows the answer for information, charging each answer its information content in bits under the model’s own prior, which suggests a new hinting method where the amount of hint is a bit budget.

7 Discussion

This work initiates the study of hinted scaling laws and posits that jointly modeling model capability and hint level enables better predictions of benchmark accuracy than modeling capability alone. We consider two prediction problems as applications: forecasting benchmark accuracy across a model family and ranking models from different families.

The main limitation of our forecasting study is the scarcity of open-source scaling ladders. Among the five model families we consider, only Delphi is explicitly a scaling ladder trained on one data recipe. Thus, the extent to which our forecasting errors are attributable to shortcomings of our methods versus artifacts of these model families is unclear. Certainly, our simple joint law is an imperfect model of the true joint effect of hint level and model capability on accuracy.

Generalizing our work beyond what we presented, developing sample-efficient methods for ranking LLM agents on benchmarks is particularly important in view of the substantial cost of running modern safety-relevant agentic benchmarks. For example, a single run of UK AISI’s cyber-range evaluation costs roughly $3000–$5000 per rollout per frontier model (AI Security Institute, 2026), and safety and red-teaming benchmarks need many rollouts to estimate long-tail risks (Angell et al., 2026; Jones et al., 2025; Wu and Hilton, 2025).11 1 The cyber-range evaluation caps models to 100M tokens per rollout. Current prices for GPT 5.5 ($30/1M tokens) and Claude Mythos priced as Claude Fable ($50/1M) then lead to costs of respectively $3,000 and $5,000 per evaluation iteration. Our ranking experiments use single-turn benchmarks, but hinting extends naturally to agentic benchmarks where a hint can replay part of a successful trajectory and let the model finish the task from that state. We do not explore hinting for safety and red-teaming evaluations in this paper, but we view this as a particularly worthwhile endeavor for future work.

Finally, both applications rely on benchmarks for which there exist verified solutions with legible reasoning for each problem. Given the rapidly expanding capability frontier of language models, we expect it will be increasingly difficult to construct benchmarks of this type that are not already saturated. Nonetheless, even in such a world, we expect hinted scaling laws will still be useful to model developers, as there will always be a need to estimate model performance from a small scale when optimizing the compute efficiency of a training recipe (Hernandez and Brown, 2020). Going beyond capabilities, hinting may also play an increasingly important role in helping model developers more precisely control complex and emergent behaviors such as reward hacking and multi-agent collusion.

Appendix A Benchmark Details

AIME.

We use the 60 problems of the 2025 and 2026 AIME I and II exams taken from MathArena. Every answer is an integer between 0 and 999. We prompt models to put their final answer in \boxed{}, extract the final answer from the response with a rule-based parser, and mark the response correct if it equals the official answer.

HLE.

From the 2,500 questions of Humanity’s Last Exam we use a 176-question subset. First, we consider only questions without images. Of these, we keep a question if (1) its answer is free-form (exactMatch) rather than multiple-choice, (2) we can generate a correct reference solution for it (Appendix B), and (3) it does not hand the model a set of candidate answers. For (3) we manually removed 14 free-form questions that ask a yes/no question, enumerate options in the question text, or ask “how many of the following”. Following the HLE protocol, we judge correctness with an LLM. We use the HLE judge prompt with its confidence field removed, since we do not ask models for a confidence score, and GPT-5.4 nano (low reasoning effort) as the judge. The judge sees the question, the ground-truth answer and the final 1,500 characters of the model’s response, and returns the extracted final answer and a yes/no verdict.

GSM8K.

We use the first 256 problems of the GSM8K test split. The reference solutions are the step-by-step solutions that come with the benchmark, with the final answer line removed; for truncation we also replace any remaining occurrence of the answer with <mask>. We grade with strict matching. We take the first number after the first “####” in the response, drop dollar signs and commas, and cast the answer to a float (effectively dropping trailing decimal zeros). We then compare it to the ground truth. A response with no “####” counts as incorrect. We include “Question:”, “</s>”, and “<|im_end|>” as stop strings.

Sampling.

Table 2 gives the sampling settings. Post-trained models use the settings their model cards recommend, and Appendix C gives the logit-mixing settings.

Appendix B Reference Solutions for AIME and HLE

Benchmark hinting methods require a correct solution to every problem. For example, both masking and truncation hinting give part of the solution to the model. Such a correct solution should not state the final answer; otherwise the model could copy it without building on the hint. This is especially relevant for masking, where the hint level HH would otherwise just be the probability of revealing the answer to the model. Thus, we make sure that the final answer is not in the correct solution.

We build the solutions in two stages. First we sample full solutions from a frontier model and keep only ones that are deemed correct by a grader. Second, we make a model rewrite each correct solution so that it does not include the final answer and stops just before it. We collect ten reference solutions per problem on both benchmarks, and each hinted rollout of a problem uses one of them.

Stage 1: sampling correct solutions.

We prompt a frontier model with the problem and keep a sample only if it is graded correct. On AIME a sample is correct if the extracted integer matches the official answer; on HLE we apply the LLM judge of Appendix A with o3-mini (low reasoning effort) as the judge. We resample until every problem has ten correct solutions. On AIME the solver is Claude Opus 4.6 with extended thinking off, or at medium or high effort. The remaining rollouts of a few problems on which Opus 4.6 rarely succeeded were sampled with GPT-5.4 with medium thinking. On HLE the solver is GPT-5.5 with medium thinking.

Stage 2: removing the answer.

After collecting correct solutions, we make a model rewrite them so they do not contain the problem answer. This second model is given the problem, the solution and the answer, and is instructed to stop before the final step and to never state the answer. On AIME the rewriter is Claude Opus 4.6 with extended thinking off. On HLE the rewriter is Claude Opus 4.7 with medium thinking. The rewritten solutions are the reference solutions used by masking and truncation on AIME and HLE. For logit mixing, the teacher uses the benchmark’s own solutions on GSM8K and these rewritten solutions on AIME (Section C.1).

Checking for leaked answers.

To check that the rewritten solutions do not state the final answer, we search each for its problem’s answer string with a regular expression. The string occurs in 19 of the 600 AIME solutions and 158 of the 1,760 HLE ones. On inspection, very few (only 4 and 2) of these state the answer; the rest contain it incidentally, as a quantity in the problem, an intermediate value, part of a larger number, or the value just before the final step.

Appendix C Logit Mixing Details

Section 2.1 describes logit mixing over the full vocabulary. In practice, we implement logit mixing by running two inference engines on separate devices and communicating only their 16 largest logits to a shared host (increasing the number of logits slows down generation). At each decoding step, we mix over the union of the two candidate sets. A candidate missing from one side receives that side’s smallest reported logit. We then sample yt∼softmax⁡(sH/T)y_{t}\sim\mathrm{softmax}(s_{H}/T) over the union, with sHs_{H} from Eq. 1 and T=0.4T=0.4. The evaluated Delphi model receives the standard 5-shot GSM8K prompt. The teacher, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, receives a chat history in which the reference solution appears as its previous answer followed by the request “Great. Can you solve it another way?” and an “Answer:” prefill, so that it continues with a fresh solution. We treat Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct’s end-of-turn token as its stop token (i.e., we mix its logit with Delphi’s stop token logit) and discard all other special tokens. We sweep 29 values of HH from 0 to 16, denser below H=1.4H=1.4, and draw 32 samples per problem on the first 256 GSM8K test problems for each of the three seeds below 102310^{23} FLOPs. For masking and truncation on Delphi we sample at the same temperature with a top-kk of 1000, 32 rollouts per problem and seed. The H=0H=0 points are unhinted runs shared by all three methods, 64 rollouts per problem and seed with top-kk off.

C.1 Logit Mixing on Post-Trained Families

Logit mixing needs a teacher that is more capable than the evaluated models and shares their tokenizer. On the Delphi ladder such a teacher is readily available. On the post-trained families the choice is less clear. Most families have their own tokenizer, so the teacher must come from the same family, and the natural candidates are its largest models. Using the forecast target itself as the teacher would leak its accuracy into the forecast. We therefore take the second-largest model of each family as the teacher, place the reference solution in its context, and mix it with every model in the family up to and including itself. We fit the joint law on every model except the largest and forecast only the largest model’s unhinted accuracy, so the target is never used as a teacher or in the fit. We run these experiments on AIME for Qwen2.5, Qwen3 and Gemma-3.

We note that this experimental setup restricts our ability to evaluate logit mixing forecasts as rigorously as the other forecasting experiments in the paper. Namely we can only evaluate forecasting from all but the largest model in the family to the largest model. Logit mixing is most natural when a stronger external teacher outside the family is available, as on the Delphi ladder in Section 4.2, and we include these post-trained results for completeness.

Raw logit mixing.    The top half of Fig. 9 uses the rule of Eq. 1. On Qwen3 and Gemma-3, accuracy rises smoothly with both the hint level and model scale, and the joint law fits both families. Qwen2.5 is the exception. At intermediate hint levels its smaller models score higher than its larger ones. This behavior is completely opposite to what we want from hinting, and accordingly the joint fit and forecast are very poor.

Flat logits and std rescaling.    The inversion comes from how the logit mixing raw rule weights the teacher. In Eq. 1 the teacher’s “effect” at a given HH depends on how confident the evaluated model is, and the scale of its logits. A student model whose logits are flat and small in scale, when summed with even a small amount of teacher logits, ends up sampling from the teacher more frequently than a student that has a sharp distribution that disagrees with the teacher. This means that larger models can receive a “weaker” hint at the same HH.

On Qwen2.5, the gap between the evaluated model’s largest and 16th largest logit grows from 14.0 for the 0.5B model to 20.9 for the 7B model. At H=1H=1, on the steps where the two models’ top tokens differ, the mixed distribution’s top token is the teacher’s on 51% of steps for the 0.5B model but only 37% for the 7B model.

One simple fix is to rescale the teacher’s logits to the evaluated model’s scale at each step,

sH​(x,y<t)j=zmodel​(x,y<t)j+H​σmodelσteacher​zteacher​(x,y<t)j=σmodel​(zmodel​(x,y<t)jσmodel+H​zteacher​(x,y<t)jσteacher),\begin{split}s_{H}(x,y_{<t})_{j}&=z_{\mathrm{model}}(x,y_{<t})_{j}+H\,\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{model}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{teacher}}}\,z_{\mathrm{teacher}}(x,y_{<t})_{j}\\ &=\sigma_{\mathrm{model}}\left(\frac{z_{\mathrm{model}}(x,y_{<t})_{j}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{model}}}+H\,\frac{z_{\mathrm{teacher}}(x,y_{<t})_{j}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{teacher}}}\right),\end{split} (4)

where σ\sigma is the standard deviation of a model’s 16 largest logits at that step, and all other symbols are as defined in Eq. 1. We call this method std rescaling. We can interpret the above equation as putting the student and teacher logits on the same scale before adding, and then scaling back up to the student model scale. Note importantly that this preserves H=0H=0 corresponding to sampling from the evaluated model, and H→∞H\to\infty sampling from the teacher.

The bottom half of Fig. 9 shows the result. On Qwen2.5, accuracy now largely increases with scale at every hint level, and the forecast error for Qwen2.5-32B falls from 6.4 to 4.8 percentage points. The forecasts for Qwen3 and Gemma-3 stay similar to their prior results.

We note that std rescaling is one of several possible corrections, which we chose after observing the Qwen2.5 inversion, and we have tested it only on AIME. We therefore present it as a possible fix for this pathology of logit mixing rather than as part of the method. Another possible correction is to sweep over rescaling the evaluated model’s logits at each hint level and take the best performing rescaling factor; this ensures by construction that every model’s hinted performance is at least as good as a model that samples tokens uniformly at random. We piloted a coarse version of this correction on the Delphi ladder, but did not pursue the approach further due to the expensive nature of the sweep. We also piloted other methods for leveraging the teacher model besides logit mixing, such as generating several candidate token spans from the student and selecting the best span using the teacher (this particular method was expensive to run, and we did not observe significant uplift for spans beyond a couple tokens in length). We leave more extensive exploration of logit mixing alternatives to future work. We note that we did not observe any pathology for the logit mixing results in the main text that use the raw rule of Eq. 1.

Appendix D Hinting and Capability Scaling: All Families

Section 3 shows the Delphi ladder and Qwen3.5 on HLE. Here we show the same analyses for the remaining (benchmark, family) pairs: Qwen2.5, Qwen3 and Gemma-3 on both AIME and HLE. Fig. 10 gives the hint and capability slices, with each slice fitted alone as in Fig. 2, and Fig. 11 gives the empirical iso-accuracy contours, as in Fig. 3. The same patterns hold. Accuracy rises smoothly with the hint level for every model, the ordering of each family is preserved, and the contours are smooth.

Appendix E Additional Forecasting Results

Figs. 12 and 13 show the joint-law fits and the forecasts for the (benchmark, family) pairs not reported in Section 4: Qwen3 on AIME, and Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 on HLE. We did not run Qwen3.5 on AIME.

Fig. 14 compares the empirical iso-accuracy contours of Fig. 3 with the contours implied by the joint law of Eq. 2. Under that law every contour is a straight line with the same slope −β1/β2-\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}, so the lower half of the figure shows what the surface would look like if the law held exactly above its floor. For Qwen3.5 on HLE the empirical contours are close to the implied ones for both masking and truncation. For the Delphi ladder on GSM8K the implied contours also track the empirical ones for both methods, with the largest deviations near the floor, where the empirical contours of masking flatten across the smaller models. These deviations are the reason we describe the joint law as an approximation.

E.1 Two-Stage Scaling Law Baseline

A natural alternative to benchmark hinting is to forecast through an intermediate soft metric rather than through a hinted benchmark. The soft metric is a continuous quantity that keeps moving while accuracy is still pinned at the floor, and the forecast is a chain of two fits, compute to the soft metric, then the soft metric to accuracy. Held [2026] uses exactly this procedure on the Delphi ladder, combining a compute scaling law with an observational scaling law [Ruan et al., 2024]. We test this method here as a baseline.

Following Held [2026], we use bits-per-byte on the GSM8K solution trace as the soft metric averaged over problems. We use the same standard 5-shot prompt. We restrict this comparison to the ten compute budgets and single seed that Held [2026] uses. All accuracies in this section, including those of the benchmark hinting forecasts we compare against, are measured on these same ten models. As a check on our implementation, our bits-per-byte measurements track those reported by Held [2026] for the same ladder closely, differing by 0.84%0.84\% on average and 2.09%2.09\% at worst across all ten rungs, despite differences in problem subset and prompt details.

We then fit two scaling laws and compose them. The first maps model scale CC to bits-per-byte with a power law in FLOPs, and the second maps bits-per-byte to accuracy with a sigmoid. Concretely:

BPB⁡(C)\displaystyle\mathrm{BPB}(C) =L∞+A​ 10−α​C,\displaystyle=L_{\infty}+A\,10^{-\alpha C}, (5)
Acc⁡(M,0)\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}(M,0) =σ⁡(b1​BPB​(CM)+b0),\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(b_{1}\mathrm{BPB}(C_{M})+b_{0}\right), (6)

where CMC_{M} is the scale of model MM.

We consider two different ways of fitting these laws and creating a forecast. The most comparable to our results in Fig. 5 is to fit both on the nn smallest models in the ladder, and evaluate on the held-out larger models. The results of doing this are shown on the left of Fig. 16, with the absolute error of the prediction shown in blue on the bottom plot. We find this method does very poorly, predicting essentially a flat line at 0, resulting in a roughly constant absolute error of 16–24 percentage points. This makes perfect sense because the second stage of the fit in Eq. 6 is simply fitting a sigmoid to a row of near zero accuracy values, the exact same problem as the H=0H=0 sigmoid we use as a baseline in the main paper.

We also consider a second setting used by Held [2026]. In this case we imagine we have access to a set of stronger reference pretrained models, which already exceed the accuracy of the largest model we plan on scaling to. It is important to note that this assumption is not realistic if one is running a frontier training run beyond the scale of any publicly available base model. However, if we assume this is possible, we can measure these models’ benchmark accuracies and bits-per-byte, and use them to anchor the bits-per-byte to accuracy sigmoid.

We show results for this reference-model fit on the right of Fig. 16. We find that the sigmoid is indeed fitted well; however, with enough held-out models the compute to bits-per-byte scaling law ends up being inaccurate, leading also to poor predictions overall. It is worth emphasizing that the downstream accuracy prediction is very sensitive to even small errors in the bits-per-byte prediction, as the three held-out models in Fig. 16 show. Indeed, the model we wish to predict, at 102310^{23} FLOPs, has only just emerged on the bits-per-byte to accuracy sigmoid, and so it makes sense that small bits-per-byte errors would cause large accuracy errors as the true 102310^{23} model sits close to the steepest point of the sigmoid.

Finally, as expected, bits-per-byte scales much less cleanly for the post-trained families than for the Delphi ladder, as shown in Fig. 15, making the method infeasible for these ladders.

E.2 Pass@kk as a Hinting Method

Here we consider pass@kk as a hinting method. Pass@kk marks a problem as solved if any of kk independently sampled attempts is correct, so k=1k=1 is the ordinary evaluation and accuracy rises monotonically in kk.

It is easy to see that pass@kk is a valid benchmark hinting method. It is indexed by a scalar, it returns the unmodified benchmark at one end of its range, and it raises accuracy monotonically as it is turned up. We therefore treat it as one more benchmark hinting method, with hint level H=log2⁡kH=\log_{2}k so that H=0H=0 is the unmodified benchmark and each additional unit of HH doubles the sampling budget. We then fit the same joint law of Eq. 2 over the resulting grid of (scale, hint) pairs and forecast exactly as before, by evaluating the fitted law’s H=0H=0 slice at the held-out scales.

Fig. 17 shows the result. The joint law describes the pass@kk slices well. In terms of forecasting, the method generally improves on the baseline. However, it underperforms our main ensembling method.

Appendix F When Can Hinting Inform a Forecast?

Not every way of making a benchmark easier helps with forecasting. As a control, consider answer mixing, a hinted protocol ωH\omega_{H} that returns the reference answer with probability HH and otherwise samples from the model as usual. Its accuracy is Acc⁡(M,H)=H+(1−H)​Acc​(M,0)\mathrm{Acc}(M,H)=H+(1-H)\,\mathrm{Acc}(M,0), so every hint slice is a straight line from the model’s unhinted score to 1. In Fig. 18 we show empirically how this method performs.

From Fig. 18 we see that the method performs terribly for forecasting. Intuitively this makes sense. Because the hint slices only depend on the accuracy of the model at H=0H=0, the hinted curves of all models with Acc⁡(M,0)=0\mathrm{Acc}(M,0)=0 perfectly overlap. This means that every set of pre-emergence models produces the same forecast, which clearly cannot be correct.

From this, we get better intuition as to what makes a good benchmark hinting method, one that separates pre-emergence models according to the difference in their underlying capability. Below we formalize this property of overlapping H=0H=0 curves, and how such benchmark hinting methods cannot exceed the performance of simply predicting based on unhinted benchmark scores.

Setup.

A ladder has models M1,…,MnM_{1},\dots,M_{n} at scales C1<⋯<CnC_{1}<\dots<C_{n} and a target M⋆M_{\star} at C⋆>CnC_{\star}>C_{n}. Write ai​(H)=Acc⁡(Mi,H)a_{i}(H)=\mathrm{Acc}(M_{i},H) and a⋆=Acc⁡(M⋆,0)a_{\star}=\mathrm{Acc}(M_{\star},0). A forecaster observes a fixed, known grid of hint levels ℋ\mathcal{H} containing 00 and the data

D={(Ci,H,ai(H)):i≤n,H∈ℋ},D=\{(C_{i},H,a_{i}(H)):i\leq n,\ H\in\mathcal{H}\},

and outputs a^⋆=f⁡(D)\hat{a}_{\star}=f(D). The standard baseline sees only the unhinted data D0={(Ci,ai​(0)):i≤n}D_{0}=\{(C_{i},a_{i}(0)):i\leq n\}. We call a benchmark hinting method unhinted-determined if there is a fixed function gg, the same for every model, such that

Acc⁡(M,H)=g⁡(H,Acc⁡(M,0))for all models ​M​ and levels ​H.\mathrm{Acc}(M,H)=g\big(H,\mathrm{Acc}(M,0)\big)\quad\text{for all models }M\text{ and levels }H. (7)

Answer mixing is unhinted-determined with g⁡(H,a)=H+(1−H)​ag(H,a)=H+(1-H)a.

Proposition 1.

Let the ladder, and with it DD, D0D_{0} and a⋆a_{\star}, be drawn from any distribution PP. For an unhinted-determined method, every forecaster ff of DD has a forecaster f0f_{0} of D0D_{0} with f0​(D0)=f⁡(D)f_{0}(D_{0})=f(D) on every ladder. Consequently, for any loss ℓ\ell,

inff𝔼P​ℓ​(f⁡(D),a⋆)=inff0𝔼P​ℓ​(f0​(D0),a⋆),\inf_{f}\mathbb{E}_{P}\,\ell\big(f(D),a_{\star}\big)=\inf_{f_{0}}\mathbb{E}_{P}\,\ell\big(f_{0}(D_{0}),a_{\star}\big),

and the same holds with the expectation replaced by the worst case over ladders.

Proof. By Eq. 7, D=Φ⁡(D0)D=\Phi(D_{0}), where Φ\Phi replaces each (Ci,ai​(0))(C_{i},a_{i}(0)) by {(Ci,H,g⁡(H,ai​(0)))}H∈ℋ\{(C_{i},H,g(H,a_{i}(0)))\}_{H\in\mathcal{H}} and depends only on the known gg and ℋ\mathcal{H}. Take f0=f∘Φf_{0}=f\circ\Phi. Since ff and f0f_{0} give the same output on every ladder, they have the same loss on every ladder, hence the same expected loss under PP and the same worst-case loss. So the best forecaster of DD is no better than the best forecaster of D0D_{0}. Conversely DD contains the unhinted cells (as 0∈ℋ0\in\mathcal{H}), so it is no worse either. □\qquad\square

In particular, fitting the joint law of Eq. 2 to the hinted cells of an unhinted-determined method is just one particular forecaster of D0D_{0}. When every fitted model scores zero without hints, the unhinted data leave the target’s accuracy completely unconstrained, so by Proposition 1 the hinted data of an unhinted-determined method leave it unconstrained too.

Appendix G Model Ranking Details

G.1 Model Sets and Ground Truth

To be able to compare ranking methods, we need to have a ground truth to compare to. Here, we describe how we determine that ground truth and how we select the set of models to rank.

We use AIME and HLE as the benchmarks. On each benchmark we start from a pool of post-trained models from several families, 32 on AIME and 25 on HLE.

Collecting rollouts.

To get an accurate ground-truth ranking, we compute an avg@kk score with very large kk. Every model has two disjoint pools of unhinted rollouts per problem: a method pool of 128 on AIME and 64 on HLE, which is the only unhinted data the ranking methods draw from, and a ground-truth pool used solely to compute the ground-truth ranking. The ground-truth pool starts at 128 rollouts per problem on AIME and 192 on HLE. We then deepen it for models that score near zero: those below 1%1\% on AIME, 14 models, receive 4,096 ground-truth rollouts per problem, and those below 3%3\% on HLE, 16 models, receive 1,024, so counting the method pool these models have 4,224 and 1,088 unhinted rollouts per problem in total. We use fewer rollouts on HLE because its grading requires a paid LLM judge. We only collect this deeper sample on part of the original model sets because it is compute-heavy and expensive to run. Deepening moves the estimates slightly, and one HLE model that was below 3%3\% at 192 samples ends at 3.0%3.0\%.

Creating a stable ranking and choosing a subset of models.

Simply ranking models by avg@kk with high kk does not guarantee a ranking is correct. Thus, we choose only a subset of the models, such that every pair of models in the set is certified at the 95% level with a Bonferroni correction over all pairs in the pool. We treat the benchmark problems as fixed, so the uncertainty is rollout sampling noise only, and form a confidence interval for each pair’s accuracy difference from binomial standard errors computed from the observed per-problem accuracies. A pair is certified if the Bonferroni-corrected 95% confidence interval on the accuracy difference between two models does not include zero. This is desirable because if the confidence interval on the accuracy difference between two models does not include zero, their ranking cannot flip. Because the intervals are simultaneous over all pairs, the Bonferroni-corrected guarantee holds for any subset of models chosen afterwards, so no further correction is needed for the choice of a model set from this model pool.

From the certified model pairs we take the longest chain of models in which every consecutive pair is certified and keep its seven lowest-accuracy members. The chosen sets are marked in Table 3. These model sets are both near zero and nearly indistinguishable: their unhinted accuracies are at most 0.81%0.81\% on AIME and 3.0%3.0\% on HLE, making them near zero. They span 0.06%0.06\% to 0.81%0.81\% on AIME and 1.7%1.7\% to 3.0%3.0\% on HLE, less than 1 and 2 percentage points respectively, making them nearly indistinguishable.

G.2 The Hint-Prior Ranking

Given a budget of kk rollouts per problem, the hint-prior ranking spends one rollout per problem on hinted benchmarks and the remaining k−1k-1 at H=0H=0. Each problem’s hinted rollout uses a single hint level in {0.1,…,1.0}\{0.1,\ldots,1.0\}, dealt in turn over a random problem order, so the levels get equal shares up to rounding. The hinted rollouts average to the hinted score Acc^1​(M,H¯)\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{1}(M,\bar{H}), where H¯\bar{H} is the pool of hint levels; the unhinted rollouts average to the unhinted score Acc^k−1​(M,0)\widehat{\mathrm{Acc}}_{k-1}(M,0), as in avg@kk. Both scores are standardized across models before being combined in Eq. 3. If all models tie on a score, its z-scores are zero and the other decides. We use Kendall’s τ\tau-a.

The weighting reflects the two scores’ errors. The unhinted score is unbiased but noisy, and its noise shrinks with kk. The hinted score is far less noisy but biased if hinted rankings do not match the ground-truth unhinted ranking. This bias does not shrink with kk. Therefore, the weight αk\alpha_{k} moves from the hinted score to the unhinted one as the budget grows. Because αk\alpha_{k} depends only on the budget and not on the data, the hint-prior ranking becomes avg@kk at large budgets even when the hinted ranking is wrong, which happens for some hinting methods, as Section G.3 shows. Below one rollout per problem there is no unhinted score, and the single hinted rollout covers a random subset of the problems.

Choice of λ\lambda.

The weight αk=(k−1)/(k−1+λ)\alpha_{k}=(k-1)/(k-1+\lambda) in Eq. 3 treats the hinted score as a prior worth λ\lambda unhinted rollouts per problem. Fig. 19 sweeps λ\lambda from 11 to 128128. No single λ\lambda is optimal. Small λ\lambda values shift weight to the unhinted score quickly, which is suboptimal if the hinted scores are correct, but large λ\lambda values keep weight on the hinted scores for too long, which is suboptimal if the hinted scores are incorrect. We use λ=8\lambda=8 throughout as an intermediate value.

G.3 Ranking with Other Hinting Methods

Fig. 20 repeats Fig. 8 for both truncation and masking. Hinted rankings largely agree with the ground-truth unhinted ranking under every method: in three of the four method–benchmark pairs, a single hinted rollout per problem ranks the models closer to the ground truth than a single unhinted one, and often by a wide margin (middle panels). Truncation is the more reliable method, with a median τ\tau over hint levels of 0.480.48 on AIME and 0.480.48 on HLE. Masking reaches 0.380.38 on HLE but is no better than an unhinted rollout on AIME, where families gain from the hint at different rates and the curves cross.

The hint-prior ranking follows this agreement (right panels). On HLE, where the hinted ranking of masking is informative, it leads avg@kk at small budgets, by 0.150.15 at one rollout per problem. On AIME, where it is not, it trails avg@kk at intermediate budgets before converging with it. Wherever hinted rankings agree with unhinted ones, the hint-prior ranking recovers the ranking from a fraction of the rollouts avg@kk needs, and where they do not, it falls back to avg@kk as the budget grows.
